10.5.7 Transparency International Ethiopia (TIE), the Ethiopian chapter of Transparency International[footnote 129], noted on its undated website that it operates a Free Legal Aid Programme which provides legal advice to members of the public, including victims and witnesses of corruption.[footnote 130]

10.5.8 The GoE MoJ reported that free legal aid services were provided through both federal and regional institutions. According to the MoJ’s October 2025 report, regional states provided free legal aid services to 75,770 people during 2024/2025[footnote 131], while federal institutions assisted a further 8,309 individuals.[footnote 132]

10.6 Witness protection

10.6.1 Article 20(4) of the Constitution guarantees the right of an accused person to examine witnesses and access evidence presented against them.[footnote 133]

10.6.2 However, the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences proclamation provides for the protection of witnesses, whistleblowers and certain family members. Under Article 3(1), protection measures apply in relation to testimony, information or investigations concerning offences punishable by death or by rigorous imprisonment of 10 years or more.[footnote 134]

10.6.3 The Criminal Procedure Code includes measures intended to safeguard witnesses during criminal proceedings. Article 67(c) provides that bail may be refused where an applicant is likely to interfere with witnesses or tamper with evidence.[footnote 135]

10.6.4 Article 4 of the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences Proclamation sets out a range of protective measures that may be provided to witnesses, whistleblowers and other protected persons. These include physical protection, secure accommodation and relocation, concealment or change of identity, restrictions on contact by accused persons, protection of confidentiality, and the use of in camera proceedings or alternative methods of giving evidence. The proclamation also provides for financial, medical, educational and counselling assistance, compensation for harm resulting from retaliation, support for family members where a protected person dies, protection against retaliatory administrative action, and immunity from prosecution in certain circumstances where information is provided.[footnote 136]

10.6.5 Article 6 of the proclamation allows an eligible person to apply directly for protection or, where they are unable to do so, through an investigator, prosecutor or another interested person acting on their behalf.[footnote 137]

10.6.6 Various laws criminalise attacks, threats and other forms of retaliation against witnesses, whistleblowers and persons who provide information to the authorities.

Article 444(1) of the Criminal Code provides that a person who assaults, suppresses or harms an individual for giving information or evidence, or for acting as a witness in a criminal case, is punishable by 5 to 20 years’ imprisonment or a fine.[footnote 138] Article 444(2) adds that where the crime ‘has entailed grave harm to the body or health of the victim or his death, the relevant provision concerning such matters shall apply concurrently.’[footnote 139]

Article 455(2) of the Criminal Code provides that a person who, ‘by violence, intimidation or by promising or offering or giving undue advantage causes another to make false accusation or give false testimony or obstructs, through interference, the giving of testimony or the production of evidence in relation to a crime punishable with rigorous imprisonment for more than two years or obstructs law enforcement officials or public servants while exercising their official duties in relation to the same crime, is punishable with rigorous imprisonment not exceeding seven years.’[footnote 140]

Article 53 of the Anti-Corruption Special Procedure and Rules of Evidence Proclamation criminalises reprisals against whistleblowers and witnesses and requires government offices to establish procedures to protect employees from retaliation.[footnote 141]

Article 12 of the Terrorism Proclamation criminalises interference with intimidation of, inducement of, or violence against witnesses, whistleblowers and persons closely connected to them in terrorism-related cases, providing for penalties of 3 to 7 years’ rigorous imprisonment.[footnote 142]

Article 16 of the Prevention and Suppression of Terrorism Crimes Proclamation No. 1176/2020 provides that [w]here the life, wellbeing of property [sic] of any person or his family is endangered for being a witness or whistleblower of terrorist crimes, he shall be given protection in accordance with the Protection of Witnesses and Whistleblowers of Criminal Offences Proclamation No.699/2010.’ Article 16(2) provides that, without prejudice to that sub-article, ‘the court hearing the case may take the following measures: a) Change the Venue; b) Cause not to publish or record the court proceedings in part or in whole or to be released in any form.’ Contravening such an order is punishable with simple imprisonment, or, where the act ‘hinders the judicial proceedings or endangers the witness’, with ‘rigorous imprisonment from one year to seven years and with fine not exceeding Birr fifty thousands’.[footnote 143]

Article 14 of the Trafficking and Smuggling Proclamation criminalises intimidation, interference, violence, threats and other reprisals against witnesses, whistleblowers and related persons in trafficking and smuggling cases, with penalties of 3 to 7 years’ rigorous imprisonment.[footnote 144]

Executive summary

In general, the state is both willing and able to offer sufficient protection to persons fearing non-state, including ‘rogue’ state, actors. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

Ethiopia has a constitution and other laws that protect fundamental human rights and penalise criminal activity. There is a functioning police force and judiciary, which are generally accessible.

However, the availability and effectiveness of protection may vary depending on the person’s profile, location and other circumstances. In areas affected by armed conflict, post-conflict insecurity, weak state presence or contested territorial control, the availability and effectiveness of protection may be reduced. It may also be difficult to access protection in rural areas. Availability and effectiveness of protection may also be reduced for perceived critics of the government, including political opponents, activists and journalists. Protection may be difficult to access for women.

See the relevant Ethiopia Country Policy and Information Notes for specific guidance and information on the willingness of the state to protect those of Amhara, Oromo or Tigrayan ethnicity and actual or perceived members and supporters of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) and Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Fano and Amhara political opposition groups and the Tigray Peoples Liberation Front (TPLF).

Each case must be considered on its individual facts. The onus is on the person to demonstrate that they are not able to obtain sufficient protection from the state.

Assessment

Section updated: 14 October 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

the state (or quasi-state bodies) can provide effective protection.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status).

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis).

2. Exclusion

2.1.1 Decision makers must consider whether there are serious reasons to apply one (or more) of the exclusion clauses. Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

2.1.2 If the person is excluded from the Refugee Convention, they will also be excluded from a grant of humanitarian protection, which has a wider range of exclusions than refugee status.

2.1.3 For guidance on exclusion and restricted leave, see the Asylum Instruction on Exclusion under Articles 1F and 33(2) of the Refugee Convention, Humanitarian Protection and the instruction on Restricted Leave.

3. Protection

3.1.1 In general, the state is both willing and able to offer sufficient protection to persons fearing non-state, including ‘rogue’ state, actors. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

3.1.2 Ethiopia has a constitution and other laws that protect fundamental human rights and penalise criminal activity. There is a functioning police force and judiciary, which are generally accessible. However, the availability and effectiveness of protection may vary depending on the person’s profile, location and other circumstances. In areas affected by armed conflict, post-conflict insecurity, weak state presence or contested territorial control, the availability and effectiveness of protection may be reduced. It may also be difficult to access protection in rural areas. Availability and effectiveness of protection may also be reduced for perceived critics of the government, including political opponents, activists and journalists. 13.7.4 The ACLED data indicate that abductions and enforced disappearances were overwhelmingly attributed to non-state actors. Of the 287 incidents recorded during the period, 90.9% (261 incidents) were attributed to non-state actors, compared with 9.1% (26 incidents) attributed to state actors at federal or regional level. Unidentified armed groups were the most frequently reported perpetrators, accounting for 27.5% of all incidents (79 events), followed by OLA/OLF (23.7%, 68 events), Fano Youth Militia (18.8%, 54 events), and the Tigray Defence Forces (11.5%, 33 events).

13.7.5 CPIT has produced the table below, based on ACLED data[footnote 232], showing abduction/ forced disappearance events by reported reason, from 1 January 2024 to 9 October 2026:

Motivation 2024 2025 Up to 9 Oct 2026 Total

13.7.6 CPIT’s analysis of the table indicates that the motive for abduction or enforced disappearance was unclear or not reported in 44.3% (127 of 287) of incidents recorded between 1 January 2024 and 9 October 2026. Where a motive could be identified, the most commonly reported reasons were ransom, extortion or financial gain (23.7%, 68 incidents), alleged support for or association with an armed group (14.3%, 41 incidents), and forced recruitment or mobilisation (13.6%, 39 incidents). A small number of incidents were linked to political affiliation or activism (2.4%, 7 incidents), ethnic or communal targeting (1.4%, 4 incidents), or retaliation and reprisal (0.3%, 1 incident).

14. Oversight mechanisms

14.1.1 For more information on oversight mechanisms including regulation, the EHRC, the office of the ombudsman, monitoring of detention centres and complaint systems, see the archived CPIN Ethiopia: Actors of protection, February 2024.

14.1.2 A report by the Government of Ethiopia (GoE) to the Working Group on the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), dated 23 August 2024, noted Proclamation No. 1307/2023 expanded the remit of the office of the ombudsman to include the investigation of administrative abuses committed by private entities.[footnote 233]

14.1.3 The same source reported that in 2023/2024, the EHRC ‘conducted 45 investigations and 32 systemic investigations related to government maladministration and 90% of administrative complaints have been resolved.’[footnote 234] The MoJ October 2025 report stated that between 2020 to 2025, criminal proceedings for human rights violations had been initiated against 19 police officers, resulting in 4 convictions.[footnote 235]

14.1.4 The ACHPR July 2025 report noted that: ‘The Commission notes with satisfaction that the EHRC is mandated to conduct regular and unannounced visits to all places of detention, including police stations and prisons, to assess compliance with human rights standards.’[footnote 236]

14.1.5 The MoJ October 2025 report stated that between 2020 and 2025 the MoJ monitored approximately 112,000 detainees and prisoners as part of its human rights protection activities.[footnote 237]

14.1.6 The OMCT 2025 report noted that victims of torture in Ethiopia had limited access to effective remedies, with legal aid, psychological support and meaningful access to justice remaining limited. It assessed complaint mechanisms as largely ineffective and lacking independence, with complainants and detainees reportedly facing intimidation and reprisals. The OMCT also noted the absence of a National Preventive Mechanism [an independent body established under the Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture with a mandate to prevent torture and ill-treatment through regular monitoring of places of detention[footnote 238] and reported limitations on independent monitoring of detention facilities, including restrictions on access by the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission.[footnote 239]

14.1.7 In an August 2025 article on the EHRC’s annual report, The Reporter noted:

‘In a surprising departure from protocol, Commissioner Berhanu Adelo, who replaced Daniel Bekele (PhD) this year, disclosed EHRC was not called to present its annual report to Parliament this time around…

‘The Commission reports it received 1,258 appeals and complaints from individuals and groups during the year, of which 416 are from Addis Ababa. More than half of the complaints concerned breaches of political and civic rights, according to the report…

‘The report states the government has opposed the Commission’s attempts to visit detention and prison facilities in the Amhara region. Its officers managed to visit just five facilities in the region during the reporting period.’[footnote 240]

Terms of Reference

The ‘Terms of Reference’ are the main topics and issues relevant to the scope of this note and provides the framework for the country information. In this note, they were:

Legal framework – relevant laws and policies

Constitution

Criminal code

Judiciary

Structure, size and composition

Judicial independence

Selection process for judges

Fair trial and due process

Legal aid and other assistance

Resourcing

Accessibility

Customary and religious courts

Organisations responsible for law enforcement

Federal security apparatus - Ethiopian National Défense Forces, intelligence services, Ethiopia Federal Police

Prison system

Regional security forces - state police, local militias

Effectiveness

Accessibility

Corruption

Human rights violations

Torture and ill treatment
